config.why: The model dissolves the disabled/everyone binary — everyone is a customer of accessibility part of the time, which is why there is no default user.

activities.anchor: so contrast checkers are part of every professional palette
activities.caption: call the contrast ceiling
activities.name: a11yMaxEst

config.prompt: The contrast scale runs from 1:1 (identical, invisible) up to its maximum — what ratio is black text on white?
config.why: 21:1 — from (1.0 + 0.05) ÷ (0.0 + 0.05). The floor is 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text and UI components.
config.context: Nobody can judge a 4.4:1 versus a 4.6:1 pairing by eye — the checker does the judging.

activities.anchor: Light-grey-on-white body text is not a style
activities.caption: constraint as design force — drag the divider
activities.name: a11yAestheticCompare

config.prompt: The brand-aesthetic objection, two readings — drag between them:

before.label: The fear
before.text: Obeying contrast rules costs the brand its aesthetic — muted palettes, compromised hierarchy, grey mush.

after.label: The reality
after.text: Large type, weight variation, spacing and a limited, high-contrast palette are exactly what strong visual design already looks like — the constraint enforces the hierarchy.

config.why: Accessibility means obeying the arithmetic, and the arithmetic happens to be good typography.

activities.caption: pair each semantic move with what it buys
activities.name: a11ySemanticMatch

config.prompt: The page that machines can read — pair each move:

pairs.right: jump heading to heading — a table of contents
the field announces its own name
'Search' for a magnifying-glass icon, not 'magnifying glass'
decoration stays silent instead of being heard twice
if it cannot be reached, it does not exist

config.why: Screen readers move through structure, not pixels — semantics power search engines and reader modes through the same tags.

activities.anchor: why lever taps displaced crosshead taps in public buildings
activities.caption: place the turning-space diameter
activities.name: a11yTurningPlace

config.prompt: Step-free access includes adequate turning space for wheelchairs — about what diameter?
config.why: About 1.5 m — and none of it helps only wheelchair users: the delivery worker's trolley and the customer's suitcase benefit too.

activities.anchor: Pellegrino Turri's 1808 machine, built for a blind countess
activities.caption: sequence the curb-cut history
activities.name: a11yCurbOrder

config.prompt: From protest to infrastructure — put the sequence in order:
items: Berkeley, 1970s — disability activists pour informal ramps at street corners
The idea goes mainstream — kerb ramps become legally required
Prams, wheelchairs, suitcases, delivery trolleys and bikes follow through them
The same economics price the market: over $13 trillion in disposable income
config.why: Features designed for the edges become infrastructure for the middle — the documented pattern, not an accident.

activities.anchor: the first hour of screen-reader use is disorienting
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the testing pipeline
activities.name: a11yCheckerSpot

config.prompt: One of these testing claims is backwards — click it:
lines: Automated checkers catch missing alt attributes, contrast violations and missing labels in seconds.
Automated tools flag roughly 30–40% of WCAG issues — the rest needs judgement.
A keyboard-only pass means unplugging the mouse and completing the task.
A screen-reader session is intuitive from the first minute — the software does the learning for you.
Testing with disabled users replaces assumptions with evidence, and participants are paid for their expertise.
config.correction: The first hour of screen-reader use is disorienting — for exactly the reasons the design should not be.
config.why: Automation is the smoke alarm; keyboard passes, screen-reader sessions and disabled users are the fire brigade.

activities.anchor: the web accessibility study that refuses to die
activities.caption: true or false — cognitive access
activities.name: a11yPlainJudge

statements.s: One idea per sentence and 'use' before 'utilise' are condescending.
statements.why: The plain-language discipline is mechanical, not condescending — and it costs the fluent reader nothing.

statements.s: Links should say 'click here' so users know to click.
statements.why: Screen-reader users pull a list of link labels — the link must make sense out of context.

statements.s: Roughly one in five adults reads below the level most websites are written at.
statements.why: Dyslexia, ADHD, second-language readers, tired commuters — cognitive load is an access barrier as real as a missing ramp.

statements.s: Timeouts should stay fixed so the system stays secure.
statements.why: Let deadlines and timeouts be extended — forgiving forms are the rule where cognitive load concentrates.
